served.stem: An autosomal recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 individuals in a population that is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the frequency of the recessive allele (q)?
served.bankWhy: This is a Hardy-Weinberg question wearing a sentence as a disguise. For a recessive condition, the word affected describes homozygous recessive individuals, so the number you are handed is q squared, not q. One in 10,000 is 0.0001, and the square root of that is 0.01. Any time a stem gives you the frequency of affected recessive individuals, take the square root first, then build p and the carrier frequency off that value.

answer.line: One allele in 100 is recessive. Affected people are q squared, so the allele is the square root.

steps: Read the word affected first. A recessive disorder only shows in aa people, so 1 in 10,000 is q squared. Not q.
Write it as a decimal: q squared = 0.0001. Undo the square: q = 0.01. Check it: 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001.
Stop where the stem stops. It asks for q, so you are done. Carriers would be the next step: 2pq, about 1 in 50.

choices.note: This is q squared, the share of people who are affected. It pulls because it is the number the stem hands you. The stem asks for the allele.
Sliding the decimal point is not a square root. The root of 1 in 10,000 is 1 in 100.
The square root of 0.0001: one allele in 100.
Rooting twice lands here: the root of 0.0001 is 0.01, and the root of that is 0.1. One root undoes one square.
This is p, which is 1 - q. Good math, but the stem stopped at q.

student.lockIt: Affected recessives give you q squared. Take the square root to get the allele.
